title: Why Boats Float
subtitle: The secret push that holds up ships
subject: Physics

pages.h: A stone sinks. A ship floats.
p: Drop a small stone in a pond. It sinks fast. Now look at a huge ship made of steel. It weighs as much as a whole town, yet it sits on top of the sea. How can that be?
This book has the answer. It is all about a secret push that water gives to everything you put in it.
pages.cap: The stone sinks. The boat floats. Water is doing something to both.
pages.fact: Did you know? A big container ship can weigh 200,000 tonnes. That is heavier than 500 jumbo jets.

p: Put your hand flat on the water in a bath. Push down. Feel that? The water pushes back up against your hand. This push is called buoyancy.
Water pushes up on everything that goes into it. It pushes up on a stone, a duck, a ship and you. The more of something that sits under the water, the harder the water pushes up.
pages.cap: Water pushes up on the boat and on the stone. Only the boat gets enough push to stay up.
pages.fact: Did you know? You feel lighter in a swimming pool because the water is holding part of you up.

p: Why does the push hold up a duck but not a stone? It is about how heavy a thing is for its size.

Take a block of wood and a block of steel the same size. The steel block is much heavier. Scientists say steel is more dense. A thing that is heavier than the same amount of water sinks. A thing that is lighter than the same amount of water floats.

v.title: Same size, not the same weight

pages.cap: Two blocks, same size. The steel one weighs about 15 times more.
pages.fact: Did you know? One litre of water weighs 1 kilogram. One litre of steel weighs almost 8 kilograms.

pages.q: Which of these will float in water?
pages.why: Wood is lighter than the same amount of water, so the water's push holds it up.

p: Roll a lump of clay into a ball. Drop it in water. It sinks. Now press the same clay into a bowl shape. It floats!
The clay did not change. Its shape did. The bowl takes up more room in the water, so the water pushes up harder. The bowl is also full of air, and air is very light.
pages.cap: Same clay, two shapes. The ball sinks. The bowl floats.
pages.fact: Did you know? A bowl shape can float even when it is made of metal. That is how a steel ship works.

p: A steel ship floats because its hull is a giant hollow bowl. Inside, it is full of air. Steel plus lots of air is lighter than the same amount of water.
Air is all around you, but it is very light for its size. The air in a whole room weighs only about as much as a big dog.

When you mix heavy steel with lots of light air, the whole thing is light for its size. That is a ship. Its walls are steel, but most of the space inside is air. Put the two together and the ship is lighter than the water it sits in.
pages.cap: Take a deep breath. Your chest fills with air, and you float higher in the water.
pages.fact: Did you know? Take a big breath in a pool and you float. Breathe out and you sink a little.

pages.h: Try it: build a clay boat
p: Can you make a sinker float?
steps: Fill a bowl or sink with water.
Roll a lump of modelling clay into a ball. Drop it in. Watch it sink.
Take it out, dry it, and press it into a wide, thin bowl shape.
Set it gently on the water. Does it float?
Now add coins one by one. How many can it carry before it sinks?
pages.cap: A clay bowl can carry a load. A clay ball cannot.
pages.safe: Ask an adult before using the sink, and wipe up spills so no one slips.

p: A ship sinks down into the water until it has pushed away water that weighs the same as the ship. Then it stops sinking and floats.

A man named Archimedes found this rule more than 2,200 years ago. People say he noticed the bath water rise when he got in. A big ship pushes away a lot of water. That is why the water near a ship rises a little.
pages.cap: A floating ship and the water it pushes away weigh the same. They balance.
pages.fact: Did you know? When a ship takes on cargo, it sinks lower and pushes away more water.

pages.q: What is inside most of a ship's hull?
pages.why: A hull is a hollow steel shell full of air. The air makes the whole ship light for its size.

p: Most things get heavier for their size when they freeze. Water is strange. When it freezes into ice, it gets a little lighter. So ice floats on water.
But only just. An iceberg floats with about nine tenths of it hidden under the sea. Only the top tenth shows. That is why ships must stay far away from icebergs.
pages.cap: Nine tenths of an iceberg is under the water.
pages.fact: Did you know? If ice sank, lakes would freeze from the bottom up, and fish could not live through winter.

p: Stir salt into water and the water gets heavier. Heavier water pushes up harder.

The Dead Sea, between Israel and Jordan, is about ten times saltier than the ocean. People float in it so easily that they can lie on their backs and read a book. Ships float a little higher in the salty sea than in a fresh-water river.
pages.cap: Salt dissolves into the water and makes it heavier.
pages.fact: Did you know? An egg sinks in fresh water. Add 4 big spoons of salt to a glass, and the egg floats.

p: Liquids can float on other liquids too. Pour oil into water. It sits on top in a shiny layer. Oil is lighter than water, so it floats.
Pour honey into water and it sinks straight to the bottom. Honey is heavier than water. You can make a tower of liquids: honey at the bottom, then water, then oil on top.
pages.cap: Two liquids that do not mix. The lighter one floats on top.
pages.fact: Did you know? Oil spills at sea float on top of the water. That is why they are so hard to clean up.

p: One of the biggest cruise ships, Icon of the Seas, is 365 metres long. That is longer than three football fields. It can carry more than 7,000 passengers, and it floats on air trapped inside its steel hull.

opts: Ice is a little lighter than water
pages.why: Water gets a little lighter when it freezes, so ice floats, with most of it hidden under the surface.

p: A submarine can float, sink and come back up. It has big tanks inside.

To go down, it lets sea water flood the tanks. Now the submarine is heavier than the water around it, so it sinks. To come up, it blows air into the tanks and pushes the water out. Now it is lighter, and it rises.
pages.cap: Deep down it is dark and cold. Submarines use air in their tanks to come back up.
pages.fact: Did you know? The first submarine was rowed under the River Thames in London in 1620.

p: How does a fish stay at one depth without sinking or bobbing up? Most fish have a small bag of gas inside them. It is called a swim bladder.
The fish adds gas to go up and takes gas out to go down. It works just like a submarine's tanks. Sharks do not have one. A shark must keep swimming, or it slowly sinks.
pages.cap: Reef fish hang in the water with help from a gas bag inside.
pages.fact: Did you know? A shark has a big oily liver instead. Oil is light and helps the shark float.

p: Air is a fluid, like water, only much thinner. Things can float in air too.

A hot-air balloon works because hot air is lighter than cold air. The burner heats the air inside the balloon. The cool air outside pushes up on the balloon, and up it goes. The first balloon flight carried people over Paris in 1783.
pages.cap: Heat makes the air inside the balloon light, and the balloon rises.
pages.fact: Did you know? A helium party balloon floats because helium is seven times lighter than air.

p: Guess first, then test.
steps: Fill a big bowl with water.
Collect ten small things: a coin, a cork, a crayon, a key, an apple, a grape, a spoon, a leaf, a bottle cap, a pebble.
Before each one, say float or sink.
Drop it in. Were you right?
Try an orange with its peel on, then with the peel off. Surprise!
pages.cap: An orange with its peel floats. Peel it, and it sinks. The peel is full of tiny air pockets.
pages.safe: Keep small things away from babies and pets.

p: A ship floats because of the air inside its hull. If a hole lets water in, the water pushes the air out. The ship gets heavier and heavier.
In 1912, the Titanic hit an iceberg. Water flooded into its front rooms. In less than three hours, it went under. Today the Titanic lies 3,800 metres down on the sea floor.
pages.cap: A ship stays up as long as its hull keeps the water out.
pages.fact: Did you know? Modern ships have walls inside that split the hull into many rooms, so one leak cannot sink the whole ship.

pages.q: How does a submarine go down?
opts: It fills its tanks with water
pages.why: Letting water into the tanks makes the submarine heavier than the water around it, so it sinks.

p: A lifejacket is light and puffy. Inside it is foam, and foam is packed with millions of tiny air bubbles.
All that air makes the jacket much lighter than water. The water pushes it up hard, and it carries your head above the waves. Always wear one in a boat. It does the floating so you do not have to.
pages.cap: The water pushes the lifejacket up, and the jacket holds you.
pages.fact: Did you know? A lifejacket made for a child can lift about 7 kilograms. That is plenty to keep a head above water.

p: Look at the side of a big ship. There is a circle with a line through it. This is the load line.

If the ship is loaded so much that the line goes under water, it is too heavy to be safe. A man named Samuel Plimsoll fought for this mark. It became law in Britain in 1876 and has saved thousands of sailors.
pages.cap: Too much load, and the ship sits too low. The line says when to stop.
pages.fact: Did you know? The load line has extra marks for salty water, fresh water, summer and winter.

p: On the space station, there is almost no up or down. Water does not stay in a cup. It forms wobbly balls that drift through the air.
Nothing floats or sinks up there, because floating needs gravity. Gravity pulls water down, and that is what makes water push up. No pull down, no push up.
pages.cap: Far above Earth, astronauts and water both drift.
pages.fact: Did you know? Astronauts drink from pouches with straws so their water does not float away.

p: People have been floating things for a very long time. The first boats were hollow logs, more than 8,000 years ago.

Later came sails, steel ships and submarines. In 1960, a submarine called Trieste went almost 11 kilometres down to the deepest spot in the ocean, and came back up. All of it works by one rule: be lighter than the water you push away.
pages.cap: Six big moments in the story of floating.
pages.fact: Did you know? Pumice is a rock from volcanoes that is so full of air holes that it floats.

items: the push that water gives to things placed in it
the hollow body of a ship that keeps the water out
to stay up on top of water or air
to go down under the water
a huge chunk of ice floating in the sea, mostly hidden under water
a boat that can travel under the water
a mark on a ship that shows how low it may safely sit

qs: If you had to build a boat out of paper, what shape would you make it, and why?
A pumpkin floats and a potato sinks. What do you think is different inside them?
Why do you think people kept building bigger and bigger ships?
